c.tagline: The world's northernmost town — polar bears, glaciers, and the Arctic at the edge of the map.

taxi.fareNote: No ride-hailing apps operate this far north; Longyearbyen Taxi runs metered cars booked by phone, and in winter snowmobiles are the main way to reach anything beyond the short road network.

emergency.note: 112 police, 113 ambulance, 110 fire. Polar bears roam beyond the settlement — a rifle and flare gun are legally required when leaving town, but firearms must be left outside shops and public buildings.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Do not walk beyond the town's polar-bear warning signs without an armed, licensed guide — bears roam outside the settlement.
Crime is virtually nil — the real hazards are polar bears, avalanche terrain and extreme weather outside town limits.

hood_desc: The compact commercial heart along Vei 300 with the Svalbardbutikken department store, the town hall, restaurants, and most hotels; the natural, walkable base for first-time visitors.
'Old Longyearbyen' up the valley by the Longyear River, home to the historic Svalbard Church, early coal-mining relics, and a quiet character; best for travelers drawn to the town's mining heritage.
An elevated residential terrace above the centre near the school and the upscale Funken Lodge, with sweeping valley and fjord views; suits those wanting calm and a short walk down to town.
The 'new town' furthest up the valley in former miners' barracks, now budget guesthouses and student housing at the trailhead for glacier hikes; best for outdoorsy and budget travelers.
The largest residential neighborhood in the middle of the valley, quiet and local with easy access to the University Centre in Svalbard (UNIS); good for longer stays and a lived-in feel.

water.note: Tap water is glacial-fed and excellent.

transit.hours: There is no scheduled town bus service; the airport shuttle runs only to meet flights, and taxis operate on call.
transit.note: Longyearbyen has no public transport network. The compact centre is walkable; taxis, rental cars, and — in winter — snowmobiles cover longer distances, while organised tours handle any trip into the surrounding wilderness.
transit.pay: Taxis are paid by card or cash directly to the driver; there is no transit ticketing system.

ferry: Seasonal expedition cruises and boat tours (summer only)

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus (Flybussen) coordinated with flights, drops at hotels in town (~15 min)

tip.r: Service is included; rounding up or ~5-10% for good restaurant service is appreciated but never expected.

food.name: Svalbard Reindeer
food.desc: Short-legged Arctic reindeer, the archipelago's own subspecies, served as rich pan-seared loin or slow-braised stew with berries and root vegetables.

places.note: Nordic fine-dining room built around Svalbard reindeer and Arctic char; reliable year-round.

places.name: Gruvelageret
places.note: Restored 1950s mining warehouse serving Arctic game; a short walk or shuttle up the valley.

places.name: Huset
places.note: Longyearbyen's legendary restaurant and huge wine cellar; reindeer is a menu fixture.

food.name: Arctic Char (Roye)
food.desc: Cold-water char from Arctic rivers and lakes, served lightly cured, smoked or pan-fried with butter sauce; the islands' signature fish.

places.name: Restaurant Nansen

places.name: Huset
places.note: Multi-course local menu praised in recent guides for its treatment of Arctic fish.

food.name: Seal and Whale Heritage Dishes
food.desc: Trapper-era plates of dark seal steak and minke whale, legal in Norway and still cooked here as a link to the old hunting and mining economy.

places.name: Vinterhagen Restaurant
places.note: Has the most comprehensive Arctic menu in town, including seal and whale.

places.name: Kroa

places.name: Huset
places.note: Serves heritage Arctic proteins as part of its long local tasting menu.

food.name: Svalbard Rock Ptarmigan
food.desc: The only bird that overwinters on Svalbard, hunted in season and served as delicate breast fillets or as ptarmigan butter and broth.

places.name: Huset
places.note: Its tasting menu famously opens with ptarmigan butter; the definitive local kitchen.

places.name: Gruvelageret
places.note: Seasonal Arctic game menu in a candlelit old mining store; book ahead in winter.

places.name: Funktionaermessen
places.note: Fine-dining takes on local birds and game when the season allows.

food.name: Arctic King and Snow Crab
food.desc: Barents Sea king crab and snow crab landed nearby, served simply cracked with lemon and butter or worked into creamy soups.

places.name: Restaurant Nansen
places.area: Radisson Blu Polar Hotel, town centre
places.note: Barents Sea shellfish is a staple of its Arctic seafood section.

places.name: Funktionaermessen
places.note: Crab courses appear on its seasonal Arctic tasting menus.

places.name: Kroa
places.note: Casual place to try Arctic shellfish with a Svalbard beer alongside.

food.name: Northernmost Bakery Buns and Cakes
food.desc: Kanelsnurr cinnamon twists, cardamom buns and cloudberry cake baked at the world's northernmost bakeries and cafes; a polar-night ritual.

places.name: Fruene Kaffe og Vinbar
places.note: World's northernmost chocolatier and cafe; famous for cakes and handmade chocolates.

places.name: Cafe Huskies
places.area: Town centre near the main street
places.note: Retired sled dogs wander the room while you eat buns and waffles; a local institution.

places.name: Svalbard Bakeri and Kafe
places.note: Fresh Nordic pastries and open sandwiches; the everyday morning stop for residents.

food.name: Svalbard Bryggeri Beer
food.desc: Beer from the world's northernmost brewery, made with meltwater from the 2,000-year-old Bogerbreen glacier; the pilsner and stout are the ones to try.

places.name: Svalbard Bryggeri Taproom
places.area: Industrial area near the airport road
places.note: The brewery itself; Friday taproom evenings and guided tastings, booking advised.

places.name: Karlsberger Pub
places.note: Long-running local pub pouring Svalbard beer beside a famously vast spirits shelf.

places.name: Kroa
places.note: The town's busiest pub for a glacier-water pint after a day on the ice.

food.name: Aquavit and Arctic Spirits
food.desc: Norwegian caraway aquavit and Arctic gins, often chilled with glacier ice; duty-free pricing makes Longyearbyen's bars unusually well stocked.

places.name: Karlsberger Pub
places.note: Celebrated for a spirits list running to hundreds of bottles; the classic nightcap stop.

places.name: Barentz Gastropub
places.area: Radisson Blu Polar Hotel, town centre
places.note: Comfortable hotel bar with Nordic spirits and cocktails; open to non-guests.

places.name: Funken Bar
places.note: Champagne and cocktail bar with valley views; the smartest drink in town.

landmarks: Svalbard Global Seed Vault
The world's doomsday crop backup juts from a permafrost mountainside above the airport, its glittering illuminated portal an unmissable photo stop (exterior viewing only).
Svalbard Museum
This award-winning museum unpacks 400 years of whaling, trapping, mining, and polar bear ecology, the perfect primer on life at 78 degrees north.
Svalbard Church (Svalbard Kirke)
The world's northernmost church keeps its doors and coffee pot open around the clock, a cozy red-brown sanctuary overlooking the colorful town.
North Pole Expedition Museum
Devoted to the airship race for the Pole, this passion-project museum tells the gripping stories of Amundsen, Nobile, and the ill-fated Andrée balloon flight.
Gruve 3 (Mine 3)
Don a headlamp and crawl into a preserved coal mine that closed in 1996, an authentic taste of the brutal work that founded Longyearbyen.
Longyearbyen's Colorful Houses and Polar Bear Sign
The rainbow-painted rows of miners' housing against stark Arctic peaks, and the famous polar-bear warning sign at town's edge, are Svalbard's signature snapshots.
Pyramiden
A boat or snowmobile day trip reaches this frozen-in-time Soviet mining ghost town, complete with the world's northernmost Lenin bust and grand cultural palace.
Barentsburg
Svalbard's still-functioning Russian mining settlement offers a surreal excursion into Soviet-style architecture, murals, and the world's northernmost brewery.
Isfjorden
Longyearbyen's great fjord serves up glacier fronts, seabird cliffs, walrus haul-outs, and beluga sightings on summer boat safaris beneath jagged Arctic peaks.
Adventdalen Valley
This broad tundra valley outside town is the gateway for dog-sledding, ice-cave tours, and northern-lights hunting, with grazing reindeer and haunting mining relics.

train.note: There is no railway on Svalbard - the old coal-mining aerial tramways are museum pieces. Longyearbyen is reached only by air, with flights from Oslo and Tromsø, or by ship. Norway's mainland rail network is operated by Vy (https://www.vy.no/en) and is over 1,000 km south.

bus.note: There are no coach routes - Longyearbyen has only about 50 km of road in total and none of it connects to anywhere else. An airport shuttle bus meets flights, and travel outside the settlement means snowmobile, boat or a guided trip with an armed guide, as polar bears are a genuine hazard.

intl.to: Barentsburg, Pyramiden & Ny-Ålesund (Norway) - summer expedition boats, Jun-Sep

ferry.note: There is no scheduled ferry to mainland Norway - everyone flies. In the summer season, boats from Longyearbyen are the only way to reach the Russian settlements of Barentsburg and Pyramiden and the fjords, and they run roughly June to September when the ice allows. Outside that window the sea route closes entirely and snowmobiles take over.

half.name: Templefjorden
half.blurb: A glacier-lined fjord north of Longyearbyen reached by boat, where tidewater glaciers calve into the water near seal and seabird colonies.

full.name: Ny-Ålesund
full.blurb: One of the world's northernmost permanent settlements, a former mining town turned research base reached from Longyearbyen by boat or chartered flight.
